1.pericope_label: I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid? For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high? Is not destruction to the wicked? and a strange punishment to the workers of iniquity? Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?

schools.summary: Ellicott frames the chapter as one grand profession of innocence rehearsing Job's life from the first, covering sins less visible to onlookers, and reads the covenant with the eyes as a guard on the avenues of desire; on the reason that follows he makes the third verse simply answer the second, compares Joseph's remonstrance, and hears the pronoun of the fourth as emphatic, the appeal made to the judge of the hearts and reins. Keil and Delitzsch render the opening as fixing the gaze upon a maiden and mark where Job stands, outside the Sinaitic revelation, holding the old patriarchal religion that Arabs who are not Moslem still call the religion of Abraham, or of the steppe.

Gill reads the covenant as a solemn engagement made in the strength of divine grace, since the eyes are the inlets to uncleanness, citing Zaleucus, who had adulterers punished by the plucking out of the eyes, and the poet's figure of beauty entering swifter than an arrow; he takes the portion from above to be God himself, the portion of his people in life and at death, and denies that any darkness hides the act from an omniscient eye.

Clarke maps the whole speech, renders the vow as cutting a covenant sacrifice with the eyes so that conscience and eyes are the contracting parties and God the judge, and argues that the maid may be an idol, on Sanchoniatho's report of the Baithulia; Wesley states the ground briefly, that Job kept from the least occasions and appearances of evil, and that however secretly the unchaste carry the matter, one stands upon a higher place and sees in what manner they act.

Henry presses the bargain: Job allowed his eyes the light of the sun and the glory of God in the visible creation on condition they never fasten on an object raising an impure imagination, under penalty of penitential tears; he says those who would keep the heart pure must guard the eyes, that fools make a mock at this sin and call it a trick of youth, and that God counts every particular step because he will call us to account, taking more exact notice of us than we do of ourselves.

debates.question: What is the maid Job refuses to think upon?

positions.position: A woman, whose beauty would draw the heart through the eye into lust
Probably an idol, since the word may name the anointed stones called Baithulia

outliers.claim: Stops to place Job outside the Sinaitic revelation altogether, in the patriarchal religion the Arabs still call the religion of Abraham or of the steppe

themes: I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high?
Is not destruction to the wicked? and a strange punishment to the workers of iniquity?
Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?

5.pericope_label: If I have walked with vanity, or if my foot hath hasted to deceit; Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity. If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands; Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the form of the seventh verse emphatic and the way meant the narrow one of strict integrity, comparing the name given the first believers; Keil and Delitzsch read the heart going after the eyes as following the lust of the eye to obtain another man's property by deceit or extortion, take the blot for a macula clinging to the hands, and observe that the word for offspring, used elsewhere of children of the body, is here the produce of the ground, the line being quoted as a proverb in the fourth Gospel.

Gill settles the vanity on deceitful methods used to cheat and defraud, renders the balance as balances of righteousness in which Job's actions would weigh even against the rule, allows that good men before Moses had revelation enough to direct them in worship and duty, and notes that sowing for another to eat stands among the judgments threatened to the disobedient.

Clarke dissents from the others on the vanity, holding that the word is elsewhere used of a false god and the whole discourse a vindication from idolatrous practice; he glosses the integrity as perfection, declares himself willing to be sifted to the uttermost for every step, thought, look and act, and alone attends to the rooting out of the offspring. Wesley makes the vanity lying and falsehood in dealings, takes the balance for an appeal to the all-seeing God, and says sin commonly enters by the eye into the heart.

debates.question: What is the vanity Job denies walking with?

positions.position: Deceit in dealings with men, whether falsehood or the grasping of unjust gain
Idolatry, the word being used elsewhere of a false god

outliers.claim: Reads the curse on the offspring as evidence that not all of Job's children were destroyed in the fall of the house

themes: If I have walked with vanity, or if my foot hath hasted to deceit;
Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity.
If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands;
Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out.

9.pericope_label: If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour’s door; Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her. For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges. For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase.

schools.summary: Ellicott passes the imprecation briefly as menial office, like a slave's; Keil and Delitzsch set the paragraph beside the one before it, so that having guarded himself against defiling virgin innocence by a glance Job is conscious of no attempt on a neighbour's marriage either, and note that the word for neighbour is the Decalogue's own.

Gill guards the first clause against blaming the woman, since the deceiving comes by a man's own wanton looking; he gives both readings of the grinding without choosing between them, calls the crime contrary to the light of nature and to the express law of God, and offers four senses of the fire, preferring the wrath of God.

Clarke notes the Septuagint's supplement, keeps the handmill after the Syriac and Arabic, reads the bowing down as the loss of all command of her own person, reports Good's rendering of the crime as premeditated and a profligacy of the understanding, and keeps the fire to the house, where jealousy brings unmixed misery. Wesley cautions that Job does not desire the imprecation but would own God's justice in it, and points out that the Hebrew has an iniquity of the judges.

Henry sets the matter inward, since all the defilements of the life come from a deceived heart, notes that Job never laid wait at a neighbour's door, answers the difficulty of the imprecation from providence by the case of David, presses the judgment home to Job as himself a judge, and joins Wesley in reading the fire as a lust that lays the conscience waste and kindles a divine wrath.

debates.question: What does it mean for Job's wife to grind unto another?

positions.position: Literal drudgery at the handmill, the work of the meanest slave
Defilement by another man, as the Targum and Aben Ezra take it

outliers.claim: Explains the second clause from Asiatic custom, where slaves were held so absolutely as property that owners lent them to guests

themes: If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour’s door;
Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her.
For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges.
For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase.

13.pericope_label: If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me; What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him? Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the charge being answered, that Eliphaz had insinuated Job favoured the rich and ground down the weak, and has Job reply that he regarded his servants as brethren, partakers of a common humanity; Keil and Delitzsch put the argument formally, that the same manner of birth by the same divine creative power and human agency makes master and servant substantially brethren with equal claims, and weigh whether the disputed word is God the One, as the Targum, the Vulgate, Saadia and Gecatilia read it, or an adjective attached to the womb, as the Septuagint, the Syriac and Symmachus construe it with the accentuation.

Gill spells out both kinds of cause, a quarrel between two servants brought before Job and a complaint against himself of work, wages, food or clothing, and says he heard each patiently and either reconciled them or passed sentence; looking forward he leaves Job at an utter loss for an excuse when God rises to defend the injured, and looking back he observes that though parents are the instruments of begetting, God is the maker of men and all are fabricated in the same shop of nature.

Clarke supplies the legal background that makes the claim remarkable, since in ancient times slaves had no action at law against their owners, who might dispose of them as of cattle and need not listen to a complaint; Job admitted his servants to all civil rights and would let them complain against himself, and at the judgment seat king and subject, master and slave stand on an equal footing with every civil distinction abolished.

debates.question: What answers the charge of oppressing the weak?

positions.position: Job's own conduct as a master, who heard his servants' causes and admitted them to rights the law did not give them
The common origin of master and servant, one maker and one manner of birth making them brethren with equal claims

outliers.claim: Reports the versions divided over whether the One who fashioned master and servant is God or a word describing the womb, the accentuation favouring the latter

themes: If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me;
What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?
Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?

16.pericope_label: If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail; Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof; (For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother’s womb;) If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering; If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep; If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate: Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone. For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the difficult eighteenth verse simply, referring its two pronouns to the fatherless and the widow already named in the passage, and corrects the closing clause of the strophe to say that Job was unable to act as the charge alleged rather than unable to endure.

Gill keeps the withheld desires to reasonable ones within Job's power, will not let the seeing of the naked stand neutral since one version has it despising and another overlooking, unpacks the lifted hand into threat, blow, signal and wrongful vote, takes the imprecation at full weight with Jeroboam's withered arm for precedent, and warns that such oaths suit only a case where innocence cannot otherwise be cleared.

Clarke sets the morsel in the ancient custom of the table, where a man who eats alone beside another as hungry is a despicable caitiff, lays six discordant renderings of the eighteenth verse side by side and asks who can reconcile them, prints Lebid from the Moallakat for its portrait of a bountiful chief, and would have judgment fall on the parts that did the wrong. Wesley notes that Job is longest on this head because here he was most accused, and says he could neither oppose that power nor bear that wrath.

Henry names the charge rebutted, reads the widow's failing eyes as a look rather than a petition, has the fatherless eat with Job and not after him since the sharpest grievance of poverty is the contempt it draws, observes that covering costs more than feeding and finds Job's comfort in sheep he came by honestly and used charitably, and makes the restraint an awe at the infinite distance, since one higher than the highest regards.

debates.question: What does the eighteenth verse say?

positions.position: That the fatherless and the widow of the preceding verses were reared and guided by Job from his youth
Unknown: the versions are irreconcilable, some making commiseration itself the nurse that reared Job, others calamity, others mercy

outliers.claim: Leaves the text to print seven verses of Lebid from the Moallakat as the portrait of the bountiful chief Job claims to have been

themes: If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail;
Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof;
(For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother’s womb;)
If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering;
If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep;
If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate:
Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone.
For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure.

24.pericope_label: If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence; If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much; If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness; And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand: This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above.

schools.summary: Ellicott ties the turn to gold back to an admonition of Eliphaz, finds it remarkable that sun and moon worship is the only idolatry Job repudiates, as though he were ignorant of the grosser kinds, and prefers to read the judge of the last verse as my judge, meaning God, doubting any reference to the Mosaic law; Keil and Delitzsch explain the kiss as a joining of lip to lip, so that turning the kissed hand toward the object of veneration is the proper act of adoration, and cite Pliny and Tacitus for the gesture and for the Syrians venerating the rising sun.

Gill treats the paragraph on gold as the figurative half of a charge of idolatry, since to make gold the ground of hope puts it in the room of the Hope of Israel; he leaves a lawful joy standing in the increase of substance, lists four readings of the sun and moon before choosing the literal one, locates the sin in a heart drawn by their magnitude to think them divine, and notes that the law of Moses made the offence capital and the Targum calls it a most amazing iniquity.

Clarke names the idolatry Sabaeism, the most ancient and most reasonable of all its species, and sets out from Calmet its three parts, the worship of sun and moon, the adoring of the sun at its rising and the moon at her change, and the kissing of the hand; he holds that to adore the lights would be to deny the God who made them. Wesley takes the judge for the civil magistrate, advanced by God and bound to vindicate his honour, and agrees that the host of heaven was the oldest idolatry and commonest in the East.

Henry states the principle that wealth is advantageous or pernicious according to how we stand affected to it, hears the real disclaimer in the clause about the hand that gained it, draws the rule that the way to weep as though we wept not is to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, keeps the kissed hand homely as a piece of civil respect still in use, and calls idolatry in effect atheism and a public nuisance that unties the bond of societies.

debates.question: What is Job denying when he speaks of beholding the sun and the moon?

positions.position: Literal worship of the heavenly bodies, the most ancient idolatry
Possibly something else: that earthly things are uncertain, or that he never credited his substance to their influence, or that he never flattered great personages

debates.question: Who is the judge before whom this idolatry is punishable?

positions.position: The civil magistrate, whose office obliges him to vindicate God's honour
Rather my judge, that is God, with no likely reference to the Mosaic law

outliers.claim: Infers from Job's silence about grosser idolatries that he seems to have been ignorant of them

themes: If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence;
If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much;
If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness;
And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand:
This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above.

29.pericope_label: If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul. If the men of my tabernacle said not, Oh that we had of his flesh! we cannot be satisfied. The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the change of ground, that Job now passes into the realm of wishes and thoughts and is far more thorough and searching with his own case than his friends had been, and takes the cry of the men of the tent for the protest of retainers who could never be satisfied with the enemy's flesh; Keil and Delitzsch read the same words the other way, taking the people of the tent for all who belonged to it, chiefly the servants though not excluding wife, children and kindred, and denying that the flesh in question is any person's.

Gill grants that Job had enemies as good men have, and precisely for their goodness, there being a rooted bitterness in the seed of the serpent; he concedes how hard the denial is, since it takes a large measure of grace not to feel a secret pleasure at an enemy's calamity, says the mouth was kept as with a bridle, and is careful that the stranger of the last verse means simply a man out of his own country, good or bad alike.

Clarke denies both the revenge and the malice behind it, turns the restraint of the tongue on the reader by asking how few of those called Christians can say as much of people who have done them mischief, and widens the hospitality past the household to the perfectly unknown man and the traveller bound elsewhere, refreshed with his bed and board. Wesley reads the men of the tent as domestics so zealous in Job's quarrel that they protested they could eat his enemy's flesh, and finds the point of the verse in Job restraining both them and himself.

debates.question: What are the men of Job's tent saying about flesh?

positions.position: That they were always fed to the full from his table, so that no one went unsatisfied
That they were so hot in his quarrel they could have eaten his enemy's flesh and never had enough

outliers.claim: Admits the difficulty of the command, that it requires a large measure of grace in exercise not to feel a secret joy at an enemy's destruction

themes: If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him:
Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul.
If the men of my tabernacle said not, Oh that we had of his flesh! we cannot be satisfied.
The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.

33.pericope_label: If I covered my transgressions as Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom: Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me, that I kept silence, and went not out of the door?

schools.summary: Ellicott will not have the allusion settled quickly, since the phrase may equally mean as man commonly does, and judges that there may or may not be any indication here of acquaintance with the narrative of Genesis; Keil and Delitzsch state the motive exactly, that Job was neither an open sinner nor, out of fear of men and a feeling of honour, a secret one, what he might have dreaded being the moral judgment of the people and the stigma attaching to families.

Gill opens by denying that the chapter claims sinlessness, since Job has owned himself a sinner and speaks here of transgressions in the plural, and what he denies is the covering; he allows the second sense of the phrase, that Job did not do as men commonly do in concealing sin through fear or shame, and takes the second verse of confession rather than of sin, that no multitude deterred him from acknowledging a fault publicly.

Clarke finds the allusion unmistakable and counts three concealments in Genesis, Adam hiding among the trees, charging the woman and charging God with having given her; he asks whether the voice of the many ever kept Job from decreeing what was right, and reports Good, who takes the verse not as a question at all but as a curse Job calls down upon himself. Wesley agrees in four words, as Adam did in Paradise.

Henry supplies the accusation answered, that Zophar had insinuated Job hid his iniquity under his tongue, and says he never made fig leaves the shelter of his shame nor kept iniquity in his bosom as a darling he could not part with; he presses the corollary that silence and retirement may themselves be the sin when a man is called to reprove wickedness or do justice to the oppressed.

debates.question: Does covering transgressions as Adam allude to Genesis?

positions.position: Yes, and unmistakably, the fall supplying three concealments at once
Perhaps not: the phrase may simply mean as man commonly does

debates.question: Is the second verse a question or a curse?

positions.position: A question, denying that fear of the multitude ever silenced him
An imprecation on himself, that he be confounded before the multitude and struck dumb

outliers.claim: Names what a secret sinner would actually fear, the stigma of families and the loss of standing in the higher circles of society

themes: If I covered my transgressions as Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom:
Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me, that I kept silence, and went not out of the door?

35.pericope_label: Oh that one would hear me! behold, my desire is, that the Almighty would answer me, and that mine adversary had written a book. Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, and bind it as a crown to me. I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, here is my mark, the signature Job is ready to subscribe, and would render the second wish as having the adversary's indictment in hand, in black and white, to be answered point by point; he reports both readings of the last verse without choosing, and observes that these verses stand out of sequence, belonging properly after the three that close the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch narrow the hearer to the searcher of hearts, since the case turns on a contradiction between outward appearance and veiled fact, and take the clause following not as a wish but as an assertion that the Almighty will answer.

Gill renders the opening as a call for a hearer and specifies the sort wanted, not the hearer Job once had as a teacher of many nor a curious idler in court but one who will hear him plead judicially; he offers three senses of carrying the indictment, preferring that Job would bear it not as a burden but as an honour, the way a man carries a sword of state, and has him forwarding the case against himself to show he does not fear the closest examination.

Clarke reads the disputed word as a pledge entered, Job binding himself under a great penalty to appear and abide the issue, and illustrates the carried indictment from a book of Chinese punishments in which the accused bear a board with the charge written on it, sometimes a plank pierced for the neck and worn for months; he has Job lay out the stations and offices of his life and go in as the sovereign commander who will not shrink from investigation. Wesley infers from the request for a written charge that Job did not live before letters were in use.

Henry keeps the wider sense of the appeal and draws the moral, that an upright heart does not dread a scrutiny and a man who means honestly could wish he had a window in his breast; he gives three reasons for wanting the charge in writing, that an unseen sin might be repented of, that a false charge could be disproved, and that the accusations would likely prove trivial once written down.

debates.question: How does Job mean to approach his judge?

positions.position: With alacrity and perfect confidence, giving a full account of his actions
Uncertain: it may instead mean with the deference owed a prince, not as an enemy but as one worthy of honour

outliers.claim: Illustrates the carried indictment from a book of Chinese punishments, where the accused wears a pierced plank bearing the charge for months together

themes: Oh that one would hear me! behold, my desire is, that the Almighty would answer me, and that mine adversary had written a book.
Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, and bind it as a crown to me.
I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him.

38.pericope_label: If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain; If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life: Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the second clause as the furrows weeping together, calls it a strong impersonation for the consequence of wrong-doing, and sums up the chapter as more than a traverse of the indictment, since Job has shown himself not merely unbroken in the moral law but exemplary in every relation of life; Keil and Delitzsch render the closing sentence along with the rest of the text.

Gill reports that some would move these verses earlier but observes that this is their order in all copies and versions, and defends it as Job's last clearing, of the tyranny and oppression his friends laid on him without proof; he allows the land to cry either over title or over usage, takes eating the fruits without money of deceit or unpaid labour, and hears behind the closing curse the original curse upon the earth.

Clarke says the most careless reader may see that these verses disturb the connection and are evidently out of place, refers the crying land to the sabbatical law by which the soil was not to be exhausted by perpetual cultivation, adds the covetous man who spends nothing on labour or manure to the list of those who eat the fruits without money, works at the two obscure plant names, and doubts that the closing sentence belongs to the book at all. Wesley takes the crying simply of title got by fraud, and names Ahab's dealing with Naboth for the worst reading of the second clause.

Henry says the whole creation groans under man's sin but that what is unjustly gained cries out against its holder, so that the ground and its furrows become his prosecutors; he sets Abraham paying for the field he bought against Ahab taking Naboth's, draws the moral that men who get estates unjustly are justly deprived of the comfort of them, and takes the closing sentence for the true end of the defence, delivered with an air of assurance, while cautioning that Job would be shown mistaken.

debates.question: Do these three verses stand in their right place?

positions.position: No, they plainly disturb the connection and belong earlier
Yes, this is the order of all copies and versions, and it makes sense as Job's last clearing

debates.question: Why would Job's land cry out against him?

positions.position: Because it was got by fraud or violence from its rightful owners
Because it had been worked without rest and its strength exhausted

outliers.claim: Doubts that the sentence closing the chapter belongs to the book, finding it absent from many Vulgate manuscripts and detached in the Hebrew

themes: If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain;
If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life:
Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended.
